newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak govt mulls measures to stem trade deficit.
newsitem.headline: Slovak govt mulls measures to stem trade deficit.

text.p: Slovakia is considering several measures to stem its burgeoning trade deficit, but re-imposing an import surcharge is at the bottom of the list, a senior official said on Tuesday.

"I have to admit that we discussed some administrative measures to fight the deficit, but we have put the surcharge at the bottom of the tray of possible tools," Economics Minister Karol Cesnek said after a regular government meeting.
Cesnek told a news conference the government did not consider a surcharge a good tool because "it would not solve the real problems of the trade deficit."
"But it (the surcharge) is still at our disposal," he said. He did not elaborate on other measures likely to be introduced.
Slovakia cancelled a widely-criticised import surcharge at the beginning of the year, after cutting it to 7.5 percent from the original 10 percent last July.
The government imposed the measure in March 1994 to help protect the economy during its transition to a market economy, started after the fall of communism in 1989.
But the surcharge proved ineffective as Slovakia's trade balance hit a deficit of 5.69 billion crowns in 1995, and accelerated to a 64.54 billion crown shortfall in 1996.
Slovakia posted a 7.06 billion crown trade deficit in January 1997, compared with a 2.13 billion crown deficit in January last year.
The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) set abolition of the surchage as one of the main conditions for Slovakia's membership of the Paris-based group.

Last week, Cesnek said the government planned to curb the deficit's expansion through increasing exports by at least eight percent and by reducing the growth of imports to a maximum 12 percent, though he gave no specifics on how it would do this.

In 1996, exports rose 6.1 percent and imports by 28.5 percent year-on-year. In January 1997, exports were up just 0.9 percent over January 1996, while imports were 22.3 percent higher year-on-year. -- Peter Laca, Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-521-8402
